claims.statement: SandboxProvider is the pluggable control-plane abstraction for sandbox backends (Modal, Daytona, E2B, OpenComputer, Vercel): it exposes name, a SandboxProviderCapabilities record, createSandbox, and the optional restoreFromSnapshot/resumeSandbox/takeSnapshot/stopSandbox methods that lifecycle decisions gate on via the capability flags.

Providers declare capabilities that the lifecycle manager must respect: supportsSandboxTimeout (extra explicit lifetimes enforced), supportsSnapshots/supportsRestore (filesystem snapshot boot), supportsPersistentResume (in-place resume of a stopped sandbox), supportsExplicitStop (API stop). resolveSandboxTimeoutSeconds throws a permanent SandboxProviderError when a sandbox timeout is configured for a provider with supportsSandboxTimeout=false.

Modal declares supportsSandboxTimeout/supportsSnapshots/supportsRestore true and supportsPersistentResume/supportsExplicitStop false, so teardown goes through snapshot plus a WebSocket shutdown message; Daytona declares the inverse (no timeouts/snapshots/restore, provider-managed persistent resume and explicit stop); E2B declares resumable pause (supportsPersistentResume + supportsExplicitStop) with no session snapshot/restore because every E2B snapshot template is durable with no TTL; OpenComputer declares the full capability set; Vercel caps session lifetimes at 45 minutes via resolveVercelTimeoutMs.

Image builds follow the create-bind-launch contract defined by ImageBuildProviderTriggerConfig: create the build sandbox, bind its provider session id via onProviderSessionCreated, then launch the build runtime; the runtime's build-complete callback is rejected until the provider session is bound. Providers needing extra fields extend the type, e.g. ModalImageBuildTriggerConfig adds cloneHost/cloneUsername.

Modal, E2B, OpenComputer, and Vercel each implement triggerImageBuild with the same ordering — create sandbox, call onProviderSessionCreated with the provider session id, then start the runtime/entrypoint — and E2B kills the sandbox if binding or entrypoint start fails rather than leaking a sandbox that can never boot.

providerSessionTimeoutSeconds in ImageBuildProviderTriggerConfig is always resolved by the adapter layer (resolveImageBuildProviderSessionTimeoutSeconds adds a 10-minute IMAGE_BUILD_FINALIZATION_GRACE_MS to the user-configured build execution budget) and providers apply it verbatim instead of choosing their own default; the Modal side clamps it with _validated_timeout_seconds.

SandboxProviderError classifies provider failures as transient (network errors, HTTP 502/503/504, RequestDeadlineError) or permanent (HTTP 400/401/403/422, config, quota); only permanent errors count toward the circuit breaker, and unknown error types are conservatively treated as permanent by the lifecycle manager.

createSandboxProviderFromEnv builds the active provider from env config per backend and throws at construction when required credentials are missing (MODAL_API_SECRET+MODAL_WORKSPACE, VERCEL_TOKEN+VERCEL_PROJECT_ID, OPENCOMPUTER_API_URL+OPENCOMPUTER_API_KEY, DAYTONA_API_URL+DAYTONA_API_KEY+DAYTONA_BASE_SNAPSHOT, E2B_API_KEY+E2B_TEMPLATE_ID); numeric/boolean envs are validated by parseNumericEnv/parseBooleanEnv and a malformed value throws at construction.

resolveSandboxBackendName maps the SANDBOX_PROVIDER env to modal (default when unset), daytona, vercel, opencomputer, or e2b, and throws on any unsupported value; the SessionDO constructs the lifecycle manager via createLifecycleManager so misconfigured deployments fail at graph construction, not at first spawn.

The image-build adapter factory reuses createSandboxProviderFromEnv to build per-provider ImageBuildAdapters, and requires the OpenComputer template only when starting a build, not when finalizing an existing session.

Daytona, E2B, OpenComputer, Modal, and Vercel are driven by native-fetch REST clients from Cloudflare Workers with zod-validated responses, per-operation timeouts (Daytona create 90s/stop 30s; E2B create 90s/snapshot 180s; Modal and Vercel start deadlines 60s and snapshot deadlines 310s), and typed not-found/conflict/API errors that providers classify into SandboxProviderError.

SandboxLifecycleManager is the lifecycle orchestrator: it evaluates pure decision functions from lifecycle/decisions.ts and executes the selected action through injected ports (SandboxStorage, SessionContextReader, SandboxBroadcaster, WebSocketManager, AlarmScheduler, IdGenerator) and the active SandboxProvider; it owns the in-memory isSpawningSandbox flag preventing concurrent spawn attempts within one request.

evaluateSpawnDecision returns, in order: skip when the in-memory spawn flag is set; resume when the provider supportsPersistentResume and the sandbox is stopped/stale with a providerObjectId; restore from snapshot when snapshotImageId exists and the runtime is compatible and status is stopped/stale/failed; skip for spawning/connecting younger than spawningTimeoutMs (stale spawns past the window are treated as dead so a fresh spawn recovers); skip/wait for ready; wait during the cooldown (bypassed for failed/stopped); otherwise spawn.

The spawn identity write is two-phase (#1589): phase 1 updateSandboxForSpawn persists a fresh sandbox id/created_at and invalidates all stored credentials, phase 2 updateSandboxAuthTokenHash publishes the new auth-token hash scoped to that identity; a deferred publisher whose reservation was replaced abandons via SpawnSupersededError without failure writes.

Before invoking the provider on spawn/restore, doSpawn/restoreFromSnapshot call stopPriorProviderSandbox, which races provider stop against a 10-second abort budget (PROVIDER_REPLACEMENT_STOP_TIMEOUT_MS) and continues to spawn on timeout; providers that cannot stop get their stored provider object id cleared instead.

isSnapshotRuntimeCompatible fails closed: a snapshot whose recorded runtime version is missing, unparseable, or below MIN_COMPATIBLE_RUNTIME_VERSION is never restored — the session falls through to a fresh spawn and the next snapshot records its version; bumping the floor retires old snapshots the same way it retires prebuilt images.

Spawn-time prebuilt-image selection (evaluateImageBuildForSpawn) requires the latest ready image to pass the runtime-compatibility floor and its repositories_fingerprint to equal the fingerprint of the session's own repository snapshot; environment sessions match their environment's image, single-repo sessions match the repo scope, and any miss (no_ready_image, missing_artifact, runtime_below_floor, fingerprint_mismatch) falls back to the base image so sessions are never blocked on builds.

When a selected prebuilt image fails to spawn, the manager marks the image build restore-failed and retries from the base image with a fresh reserved spawn identity (the failed attempt may have created a provider-side sandbox, so rotating the token hash and sandbox id locks an orphan out of the Durable Object).

restoreFromSnapshot seeds the snapshot's runtime version as the sandbox's authoritative runtime (the restored sandbox runs the snapshot's binaries regardless of what the provider exports at launch) and falls back to a fresh spawn when the provider lacks restoreFromSnapshot; resumeSandbox uses updateSandboxForResume without rotating auth identity and falls back to a fresh spawn when the provider reports shouldSpawnFresh (e.g. sandbox no longer exists).

triggerSnapshot stamps the snapshot_image_id together with the sandbox's current runtime_version, because the image carries that runtime's binaries and a later restore is gated on it; non-terminal sandboxes move to snapshotting (broadcast) during the call and are restored to their previous status unless the reason is heartbeat_timeout.

handleAlarm evaluates connecting timeout (120s, applying to both connecting and spawning), heartbeat staleness (90s = 3x 30s interval), and inactivity (10-minute default with a 5-minute extension when clients are connected); inactivity timeout sets status stopped first to block reconnection attempts, then either provider-managed stop (resumable providers) or snapshot-then-shutdown (non-resumable), sending a shutdown WebSocket message when the provider cannot stop via API.

Provider stop semantics differ by reason and provider: Daytona deletes on respawn and stops otherwise; E2B kills on terminal reasons (connecting_timeout, respawn) and pauses otherwise (TERMINAL_STOP_REASONS, so a failed session is not orphaned); OpenComputer deletes on respawn (with the secret store) and hibernates otherwise; Vercel stops with 404 treated as success; Modal has no stopSandbox and relies on the shutdown WebSocket message.

The sandbox environment contract is centralized in sandbox-env.ts: SESSION_CONFIG carries the canonical snake_case SessionConfigPayload decoded by the runtime (fixing providers' hand-rolled divergences like Daytona dropping mcp_servers); boot-mode markers IMAGE_BUILD_MODE/RESTORED_FROM_SNAPSHOT/FROM_REPO_IMAGE/REPO_IMAGE_SHA are control-plane-owned; and the repo-image callback env (OI_REPO_IMAGE_BUILD_ID, OI_REPO_IMAGE_CALLBACK_URL, OI_REPO_IMAGE_FAILURE_CALLBACK_URL, OI_REPO_IMAGE_CALLBACK_TOKEN, OI_REPO_IMAGE_PROVIDER_SESSION_ID) is pinned by value to the shared manifest with user secrets scrubbed via RESERVED_REPO_IMAGE_CALLBACK_ENV_KEYS.

E2B pins platform env on every sandbox (HOME=/home/user for the non-root runtime, PYTHONPATH=/app, NODE_PATH, OI_SCM_CRED_CACHE_DIR, and SANDBOX_VERSION because E2B does not propagate Dockerfile ENV) and starts the supervisor with a single detached envd exec (nohup python -m sandbox_runtime.entrypoint >/tmp/oi-supervisor.log 2>&1 &); only the provider session id is allowed on E2B's platform-logged command line, so session secrets ride create-time envVars exclusively.

Code-server and VNC passwords are derived deterministically per sandbox id via deriveCodeServerPassword/deriveVncPassword over the control-plane sandboxAccessPasswordSecret (domain-separated), so persistent resumes re-derive the same credentials; shared service-port defaults and user tunnel-port validation/capping live in port-resolution.ts (MAX_TUNNEL_PORTS, raw VNC port reserved).

The infra packages (modal-infra, daytona-infra, e2b-infra, opencomputer-infra) are build-time only: they produce the provider base artifact (Modal image, Daytona base snapshot, E2B template, OpenComputer snapshot) that sandboxes boot from, while all runtime operations go through the control plane's REST clients; every package pins the same toolchain (OpenCode 1.18.18, code-server 4.109.5, agent-browser 0.21.2, ttyd 1.7.7) and bakes packages/sandbox-runtime into the image.

Modal's base image embeds CACHE_BUSTER = RUNTIME_VERSION in a no-op echo so bumping it force-rebuilds the image layer; it is one generation sequence shared by every image-build provider and MIN_REBUILD_RUNTIME_VERSION gates which prebuilt images get rebuilt onto it. Modal is deployed by running `uv run python deploy.py --build-sandbox-image` before `uv run modal deploy deploy.py` — never deploying src/app.py directly.

Modal's sandbox/manager.py boots sandboxes from the base image, a repo image (modal.Image.from_id + FROM_REPO_IMAGE=true), or a snapshot image (RESTORED_FROM_SNAPSHOT=true); snapshots use native snapshot_filesystem with a 300s timeout and persist indefinitely; build_session.py runs image-build sandboxes with IMAGE_BUILD_MODE=true and the callback env, started via api_start_build_sandbox only after the provider session is bound in D1.

Daytona's base snapshot is seeded by packages/daytona-infra (python -m src.bootstrap --force), which rebuilds the named DAYTONA_BASE_SNAPSHOT and polls up to 300s after delete because Daytona's snapshot.delete returns before the backend finishes; the bootstrap needs DAYTONA_API_KEY with Snapshots: Read/Write/Delete permissions.

The E2B template (e2b.Dockerfile + build-template.py) is built programmatically via the E2B Template SDK authenticated with the same E2B_API_KEY the runtime uses; its start command is an inert `sleep infinity` kept only so the READY_CMD gates the build on the baked toolchain — the control plane execs the supervisor on every create — and build-template.py pre-warms the template to avoid a vendor-confirmed slow first spawn.

The OpenComputer runtime snapshot is built by packages/opencomputer-infra/src/build-template.ts via the @opencomputer/sdk Snapshots API with a deterministic cacheKey, --dry-run to print the manifest, and OPENCOMPUTER_API_URL/OPENCOMPUTER_API_KEY/OPENCOMPUTER_BUILDER_MEMORY_MB env; the resulting OPENCOMPUTER_TEMPLATE is required to start OpenComputer sandboxes but not to finalize existing sessions.

The Vercel base runtime snapshot is built at build time inside a temporary Vercel sandbox (buildVercelBaseSnapshot): the bootstrap script and runtime archive are uploaded, applied, the filesystem snapshotted, and the session stopped in a finally; VERCEL_SANDBOX_VERSION = SANDBOX_RUNTIME_VERSION is injected at spawn because the base snapshot bakes no SANDBOX_VERSION and without it every sandbox would report an unknown runtime and its snapshots would be unrestorable.

Dead-sandbox policy is a deny-list, not an allowlist: DEAD_SANDBOX_STATUSES = {stopped, stale, failed}, so an unknown future status is treated as live; isSandboxReconnectBlockedStatus blocks bridge reconnects for stopped/stale but deliberately allows failed, because a slow boot can outlive the connecting watchdog and self-heal when its bridge arrives.

The warm decision proactively spawns a sandbox when the user starts typing: evaluateWarmDecision skips only when a WebSocket is connected, a spawn is already in progress, or status is spawning/connecting — deliberately not coercing a missing sandbox row so warm-on-typing still spawns for sessions with no sandbox yet.
